title: How would you design an OTP service that survives a login spike (50k RPS onto a 10k/min SMS provider): the key fix is the "Resend" button re-sends the EXISTING valid OTP instead of generating a new one, plus multi-level rate limiting, queue buffering with TTL/priority to absorb the spike, provider failover, and TOTP/email as provider-independent fallbacks?
shortTitle: How would you design an OTP service that survives a login spike
keyPoints: The key fix is making the Resend button re-send the existing valid OTP instead of generating a new one, killing retry-storm amplification.
Multi-level rate limiting (per-user, per-IP, per-provider, global) protects at different scopes.
A TTL-and-priority queue smooths the burst to the provider's sustainable rate, discarding expired OTPs automatically.
Multi-provider failover with a token bucket per provider routes to a provider that still has capacity.
TOTP (time-based one-time password) needs no SMS and adds zero provider load, making it the strategic long-term fallback.
Store OTPs in Redis with expiry as TTL so the Resend check is a cheap key lookup.
The through-line is: reduce provider calls first, then pace what remains, then fall back to channels that need no provider.

s1_definition.oneliner: Survive an OTP spike by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP, then add multi-level rate limiting, a TTL-and-priority queue, multi-provider failover, and TOTP/email as provider-independent fallbacks.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Resend fix** – The biggest single reduction: if a valid OTP already exists, re-send it instead of minting a new one, collapsing retry-storm amplification.
- **Multi-level rate limiting** – Per-user (3 OTPs in 5 minutes), per-IP (escalating to CAPTCHA), per-provider (token bucket at contractual rate), global cap.
- **TTL queue** – A priority queue with TTL absorbs the burst; expired send jobs are discarded rather than sending stale codes.
- **Provider failover** – Multiple SMS providers each with their own token bucket; fail over to the next provider that still has tokens.
- **TOTP fallback** – A time-based OTP generated on the user's device needs no network call and zero provider load.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India's branch can only hand out ten thousand paper tokens per minute, but during a festival fifty thousand customers per second rush the counter. If every impatient customer who already has a valid token keeps re-asking for a new one, the counter is instantly overwhelmed. The single biggest fix is: if you already hold a valid token, the clerk re-hands you the same one, not a fresh one. Then add crowd control, a waiting line, a backup printer, and a mobile-app token that needs no printer at all.

sections.s6_takeaway:
An OTP service that survives a login spike is fundamentally a demand-supply mismatch problem. At National Bank of India, a festival promotion produced 50,000 OTP requests per second onto an SMS provider that could handle 10,000 per minute. The single most effective fix was making the Resend button re-send the existing valid OTP instead of generating a new one. Impatient users like Rajesh tapping Resend five times had been generating five full provider calls; after the fix, one OTP was generated and the re-sends were cheap, paced operations that collapsed the retry storm.

On top of that, Pankaj layered multi-level rate limiting: per-user (3 in 5 minutes), per-IP (escalating to CAPTCHA), per-provider (token bucket at the contractual rate), and a global cap. A TTL-and-priority queue absorbed the burst and drained at the provider's sustainable rate, discarding expired jobs that would have sent stale codes. High-value actions like Priya's large transfer jumped ahead of routine logins in the priority queue.

Provider failover routed to the next provider that still had capacity when the primary's token bucket was empty, and TOTP for enrolled customers like Pankaj let them log in with zero provider involvement. The through-line is: reduce provider calls first (Resend fix), then pace and route what remains (queue, failover), then fall back to channels that need no provider (TOTP, email).

Remember one sentence: Survive an OTP spike by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP to kill retry-storm amplification, then layer multi-level rate limiting, a TTL-and-priority queue, multi-provider failover, and TOTP as the provider-independent fallback.
